## Solution

We evaluate \( I = \oint_{|z|=1} \dfrac{\cos z}{z(e^{z}-1)}\,dz \) via the residue theorem.

### Singularities inside \(|z|=1\)

The denominator \(z(e^z-1)\) vanishes when \(z=0\) or \(e^z=1\), i.e. \(z=2\pi i k,\ k\in\mathbb{Z}\). Since \(|2\pi i|=2\pi>1\), the only singularity inside the unit circle is \(z=0\).

### Nature of the singularity at \(z=0\)

Both factors \(z\) and \(e^z-1 = z + z^2/2 + \cdots\) vanish at \(z=0\), so \(z(e^z-1)\) has a zero of order 2 there. Since \(\cos(0)=1\neq 0\), the integrand has a **pole of order 2** at \(z=0\).

### Laurent expansion and residue

Write
\[
z(e^z-1)=z^2\!\left(1+\tfrac{z}{2}+\tfrac{z^2}{6}+\tfrac{z^3}{24}+\cdots\right).
\]

Let \(g(z)=\dfrac{1}{1+z/2+z^2/6+z^3/24+\cdots}\). Setting \(u=\tfrac{z}{2}+\tfrac{z^2}{6}+\cdots\) and using \(\frac{1}{1+u}=1-u+u^2-\cdots\):

\[
u=\tfrac{z}{2}+\tfrac{z^2}{6}+\cdots,\qquad u^2=\tfrac{z^2}{4}+\cdots,\qquad u^3=\tfrac{z^3}{8}+\cdots
\]

\[
g(z)=1-\left(\tfrac{z}{2}+\tfrac{z^2}{6}+\tfrac{z^3}{24}\right)+\left(\tfrac{z^2}{4}+\tfrac{z^3}{6}\right)-\tfrac{z^3}{8}+\cdots
=1-\tfrac{z}{2}+\tfrac{z^2}{12}+0\cdot z^3+\cdots
\]

Now multiply by \(\cos z = 1-\tfrac{z^2}{2}+\tfrac{z^4}{24}-\cdots\):

\[
\cos(z)\,g(z)=\left(1-\tfrac{z^2}{2}+\cdots\right)\!\left(1-\tfrac{z}{2}+\tfrac{z^2}{12}+\cdots\right)
=1-\tfrac{z}{2}+z^2\!\left(\tfrac{1}{12}-\tfrac{1}{2}\right)+\cdots
=1-\tfrac{z}{2}-\tfrac{5z^2}{12}+\cdots
\]

Therefore
\[
f(z)=\frac{\cos z}{z(e^z-1)}=\frac{1}{z^2}\!\left(1-\tfrac{z}{2}-\tfrac{5z^2}{12}+\cdots\right)=\frac{1}{z^2}-\frac{1}{2z}-\frac{5}{12}+\cdots
\]

The coefficient of \(1/z\) gives the residue:
\[
\operatorname{Res}_{z=0} f(z)=-\frac{1}{2}.
\]

### Applying the residue theorem

\[
I = 2\pi i\cdot\operatorname{Res}_{z=0} f(z)=2\pi i\cdot\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=-\pi i.
\]

\[
\boxed{I=-\pi i}
\]

        = (1/z²)(1 - z/2 + z²/12 - z²/2 + ...)
        = (1/z²)(1 - z/2 + z²(1/12 - 1/2) + ...)
        = (1/z²)(1 - z/2 - 5z²/12 + ...)
        = 1/z² - 1/(2z) - 5/12 + ...

f(z) = cos(z) / [z²(1 + z/2 + z²/6 + ...)]
     = (1/z²) · cos(z) · [1/(1 + z/2 + z²/6 + ...)]

Let g(z) = 1/(1 + z/2 + z²/6 + z³/24 + ...)

1 + z/2 + z²/6 + z³/24 + ... Let u = z/2 + z²/6 + z³/24 + ...
g = 1 - u + u² - u³ + ...

u = z/2 + z²/6 + z³/24 + ...
u² = z²/4 + 2·(z/2)(z²/6) + ... = z²/4 + z³/6 + ...
u³ = z³/8 + ...

g = 1 - (z/2 + z²/6 + z³/24) + (z²/4 + z³/6) - z³/8 + ...
  = 1 - z/2 + z²(-1/6 + 1/4) + z³(-1/24 + 1/6 - 1/8) + ...
  = 1 - z/2 + z²(1/12) + z³(-1/24 + 4/24 - 3/24) + ...
  = 1 - z/2 + z²/12 + z³(0) + ...
  = 1 - z/2 + z²/12 + ...

Now cos(z) · g(z) = (1 - z²/2 + z⁴/24 - ...)(1 - z/2 + z²/12 + ...)
= 1·1 + 1·(-z/2) + 1·(z²/12) + (-z²/2)·1 + (-z²/2)·(-z/2) + ...
= 1 - z/2 + z²/12 - z²/2 + z³/4 + ...
= 1 - z/2 + z²(1/12 - 1/2) + z³/4 + ...
= 1 - z/2 - 5z²/12 + z³/4 + ...

So f(z) = (1/z²)(1 - z/2 - 5z²/12 + ...) = 1/z² - 1/(2z) - 5/12 + ...

Residue = -1/2.

I = 2πi · (-1/2) = -πi.

The answer is -πi.
